title: Burst provisioning & steady-state SLA discovery - Candela Networks
next_steps: SE to run 1h token/sec microbench on customer's sample model and return results
Send security pack (SOC2 + network diagrams) to Lena
Schedule 90-min technical pilot kickoff next Wednesday with on-call SREs
summary: Initial deep discovery between Redwood AE/SE and Candela Networks platform/SRE/infra. Focus: provision strategy for unpredictable token bursts vs steady-state p95 SLAs; tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private (VPC/on-prem). Agreed to run short microbenchmarks and share security docs. Next: pilot kickoff and pricing overview for reserved burst capacity.
topics: p95 latency targets and how to measure
questions: Can Redwood guarantee p95 < 600ms for 512-token streaming with 20 concurrent clients?
How does dedicated burst capacity billing work?
Can KV cache prefix hits be preserved across restarts in our private deployment?
What's the fallback chain if Dedicated capacity runs out during a surge?
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-12-24 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Samir (Candela Head of Platform), Janelle (ML infra), Tom (SRE), Lena (Security)

Summary: see summary field above; quick recap at end with next steps.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for taking time — merry almost holidays — quick intros then we'll jump in. 
[00:17] Samir: yeah thanks, appreciate it. Samir, head of platform at Candela. We run customer-facing inference for network diagnostics, lots of unpredictable spikes. 
[00:28] Janelle: hi all, Janelle, we own the model infra and pipelines. Important for us: we need predictable p95 latencies and cost controls. 
[00:40] Diego: great, can you paint a quick picture of what a typical burst looks like? tokens per second, concurrent streams? 
[00:48] Janelle: typical steady-state is 5–8 qps for the 4B transformer we use, but bursts hit 220–350 parallel sessions for a few minutes when customers run bulk scans. Token lengths vary 150–700 tokens, average ~320. 
[01:10] Tom: and we stream responses back to customers, so partial token latency matters — p95 end-to-end must be < 700ms, ideally 500ms for premium customers. 
[01:25] Priya: noted. For streaming p95 targets, we usually look at token latency (time-to-first-token and inter-token). Do you have client-side instrumentation? 
[01:35] Samir: rudimentary tracing, but we'll provide sample traces. We want to understand whether hosted Redwood can hit those numbers or if we should go dedicated or private. 
[01:46] Diego: okay, cool. Quick distinction: Hosted is simplest and fastest to onboard but shared pools so burst isolation is probabilistic; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with burst/overprovision configs; Private (VPC/on-prem) gives full network control and KMS integration but involves deployment lead time. 
[02:10] Janelle: what about graceful degradation? If we hit a surge and dedicated is saturated, what happens to latency and user experience? 
[02:18] Diego: we have routing policies — automatic fallback to a cheaper model variant or another region. Streaming can fall back to batch generation with partial updates but that impacts first-token latency. 
[02:32] Tom: can you quantify that? like 95th increases by what factor? 
[02:36] Diego: ballpark: fallback to a smaller model might double the p95 for first token but keep token throughput up. Another option is throttling with queued requests and streaming partial placeholders. It depends on your critical path. 
[02:52] Samir: our SLAs are strict; if the premium customers see doubled latency, we'll get escalated. So we need precise numbers. 
[02:59] Maya: agreed. Let's talk benchmarks: what you'd like us to run and what metrics will convince you. 
[03:06] Janelle: we want token/sec sustained and under-burst peak. Also p95 first-token and p95 tail (last-token) for streaming. And failover behavior under a simulated Dedicated saturation. 
[03:20] Priya: perfect. We'll ask for a sample model artifact — is it open model or fine-tuned? 
[03:27] Janelle: it's a fine-tuned open-arch 6B variant, largely transformer-decoder, standard kv cache. We can share a small anonymized checkpoint. 
[03:37] Diego: good. Two practical notes: 1) microbench results vary with tokenization and batch composition; please share representative prompts. 2) we'll run tests on Redwood Dedicated profile, Hosted, and a Private pre-prod if network allows. 
[03:52] Samir: private pre-prod would need a network enclave—how long to spin that? 
[03:57] Priya: for a lightweight pilot VPC deployment with our control plane, 3–5 business days if we have networking details and creds. On-prem is longer. 
[04:07] Tom: security: Lena, can you outline must-haves? 
[04:10] Lena: SOC2 attestation, encrypted-at-rest with KMS, SSO/SAML integration, audit logs with request-level tracing, and edgeless IP allowlist. Also, we need to confirm whether KV cache resides in encrypted volume and persistence guarantees across restarts. 
[04:26] Diego: KV cache is persisted to encrypted volumes in Dedicated and Private; Hosted uses ephemeral node-local caches with cross-shard cache warming and prefix caching. We can share the persistence behavior doc. 
[04:38] Lena: important — if cache warms are lost after scale-down, p95 for cold starts spikes. 
[04:44] Priya: we often recommend prefix caching and pre-warming for known heavy prefixes. Also, quantization profile can reduce latency and memory footprint if accuracy is acceptable. 
[04:55] Janelle: what's the usual p95 improvement when going from float16 to 4-bit quant? 
[05:00] Diego: typically 20–40% faster inference and less memory, but depends on kernel support and sequence length. Some models see single-digit percentile regressions in output quality; we'll validate. 
[05:15] Samir: cost question — Dedicated reserved capacity with burst windows, how's that priced? Is there a bill for ephemeral burst above committed? 
[05:24] Maya: yes, reserved capacity has a base commit and then burst units billed at a different (higher) rate. We can propose a hybrid: base reserved for steady-state and a purchasable burst allowance for seasonal spikes. 
[05:39] Tom: do you support autoscaling down to zero for Dedicated? 
[05:43] Diego: we don't do zero for Dedicated — minimum pool sizing applies for reservation guarantees. Hosted can handle elastic zero-to-X but with cold start implications. 
[05:55] Janelle: about streaming semantics — can streaming responses be consumed while fallback or reroute occurs? Any duplication or gap risk? 
[06:03] Priya: we stitch tokens with sequence IDs and can resume streams; there's a tiny window where the client might see a repeated token if connection reestablishes — we can handle idempotency at the API level. 
[06:16] Samir: good. Let's talk target numbers: we want p95 end-to-end under 600ms for 512-token streams at 20 concurrent streams per second in steady-state, and under 1.2s p95 during bursts of 250 concurrent sessions. Are those feasible? 
[06:33] Diego: for Hosted it's risky. Dedicated on A100-class pools with optimized kernels, and prefix caching, seems plausible for steady-state; during huge bursts you'd need pre-warmed burst pool or spillover strategies. 
[06:46] Tom: how would you implement pre-warmed burst pools? 
[06:50] Diego: you reserve a smaller set of warm instances kept online with KV cache primed; when an incoming surge starts, traffic routing shifts to the warm pool. That avoids cold-start p95 spikes. 
[07:03] Janelle: what's the warm pool memory/cost overhead? 
[07:07] Maya: warm pools are billed like active Dedicated nodes. So yes, cost overhead. We'll model tradeoffs in the pricing sheet. 
[07:18] Samir: can we have a policy that keeps warm pool on only during known windows and auto-scale with predictive warm-up? 
[07:25] Priya: yes, we can use traffic-based predictive warmers. You feed historical traffic windows and we pre-warm few minutes in advance. 
[07:33] Tom: how do you observe p95 across client regions? We operate in NA + EU and need regional routing. 
[07:39] Diego: Redwood Console shows per-region p95 and token-level breakdowns. You can set routing policies by client region to nearest pool or failover to another region. 
[07:49] Lena: network egress — can we keep data from leaving EU for EU customers? 
[07:53] Maya: yes, with Private (VPC) deployments you can control region placement and data residency; Hosted also has region-restricted plans but Dedicated gives the clearest isolation. 
[08:03] Samir: let's talk measurement methodology. If you run benchmarks, we need consistent tokenization, synthetic vs real prompts, and client-side latencies included. 
[08:12] Diego: agreed. We'll run two suites: 1) synthetic steady-state with fixed prompt lengths and concurrency; 2) recorded real-traffic replay derived from your traces to exercise variance. We'll return token/sec, time-to-first-token, inter-token latency percentiles, memory/CUDA metrics, and NVidia profilers if allowed. 
[08:31] Janelle: what about warm vs cold start tests? 
[08:33] Priya: we'll run cold start scenarios by cycling node pools and measuring first N requests. 
[08:39] Tom: during tests, will you simulate Dedicated saturation and measure fallback chain? 
[08:43] Diego: yes, we can artificially cap the Dedicated pool and route overflow to Hosted or cheaper variants to measure impact. 
[08:51] Samir: perfect. Any gotchas with our model architecture? KV cache size, offload to CPU, etc? 
[08:56] Priya: large KV caches can increase memory pressure; we support sharded KV and offloading strategies, but offload adds latency. We'll check your sequence length distributions. 
[09:06] Janelle: regulatory question: if we use Dedicated in a cloud region, do we have to manage keys or can Redwood integrate with our KMS? 
[09:13] Diego: Private and Dedicated support customer-managed keys (bring-your-own-KMS). Hosted offers Redwood-managed KMS by default but can do enterprise KMS integrations for accounts with contracts. 
[09:25] Lena: we need audit logs with per-token request IDs retained 12 months. Is that feasible? 
[09:31] Maya: long retention is part of our enterprise add-ons — we can provide log retention and export hooks to your SIEM. We'll include costs in the security pack. 
[09:42] Samir: switching to concrete commitments — what's the timeline to get the microbench results and pilot? 
[09:48] Diego: if you share the sample model and prompt set today, we can run microbench in 48–72 hours and deliver a short report. For a pilot VPC build, 3–5 business days after network info. 
[10:00] Maya: we'll also prepare a pricing sketch that mixes reserved steady-state with a burst allowance. 
[10:06] Janelle: are there reference customers you can point to with similar burst patterns? 
[10:10] Maya: we can share anonymized case studies; will add to the follow-up. 
[10:14] Tom: on telemetry — what's the overhead of your tracing? Will it affect p95? 
[10:18] Priya: minimal; we sample at configurable rates. Full tracing has slight CPU overhead but doesn't materially change inference p95 on GPU-bound workloads. 
[10:26] Samir: ok let's do the checklist: sample model + prompts, network details for VPC, SAML metadata for SSO, and a list of spike windows. Anything else? 
[10:35] Janelle: also include the benchmark harness and the test client so we can reproduce. 
[10:39] Diego: yes we'll commit the harness and an infra-as-code snippet for the pilot. 
[10:44] Lena: and add SOC2 report + KMS integration doc. 
[10:47] Maya: noted. 
[10:50] Priya: on the architecture side, one more note: for streaming p95 we recommend continuous batching with small micro-batches; it gives throughput without hurting first-token too much. We'll simulate that. 
[11:02] Samir: any risk when using quantization in streaming mode? 
[11:06] Diego: quantization can increase per-step jitter, but in many cases it's still within p95 targets. We'll include quality regressions in the report. 
[11:15] Tom: final question — if Dedicated fails and fallback to Hosted triggers, what about customer data residency? 
[11:22] Maya: fallback can be constrained by policy; if your policy forbids cross-region or cross-environment fallbacks with certain data classes, we can block fallback and instead queue or use degraded responses. We'll need to map data classes. 
[11:36] Samir: okay great, that maps to our concerns. Any blockers? 
[11:40] Maya: only that we get the model + prompts + network/SAML data to proceed. We'll also send an NDA for the model artifact exchange if needed. 
[11:50] Janelle: sounds good. 
[11:55] Maya: quick recap of next steps: Redwood to run microbench + share results within 72h; Redwood to send security pack and pricing sketch; schedule 90-min pilot kickoff next Wednesday. Customer to share model, prompts, network, SAML metadata, and a list of peak windows. 
[12:12] Samir: confirmed. Thanks team. Happy holidays. 
[12:20] Maya: thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invite and the checklist. Bye.

Notes on transcription: several acronyms transcribed imperfectly (kv cache sometimes as K V cash, SAML as samel), minor speaker label jumps; natural filler words preserved.
